> 善行無轍跡；善言無瑕謫；善數不用籌策.

Chapter 26 was all prohibition: don't be light, don't be agitated. Once the prohibitions are in place, the obvious question appears — then what should one do?

Chapter 27 answers it, and the answer is strange: five skills, four absences, two "doesn't need."

Laozi spends the entire chapter describing what is not used. Not once does he say what is used.

That is the argument. Not a better toolkit — rather, at that point the tools don't need to be carried.

## 善行無轍跡

Good walking leaves no rut. 轍 is the wheel track — the mark that says exactly where you went.

A track is what makes movement legible: it tells everyone which way you came and where you can be followed. The good walker leaves none, not because he is hiding, but because the walking was fitted to the ground rather than imposed on it.

## 善言無瑕謫

Good speech leaves no flaw to pick. 瑕 is a jade flaw; 謫 is a fault that can be blamed.

Speech that leaves no opening is not guarded speech — it is speech with nothing extra in it. The openings that get attacked are usually not the content; they are the surplus: the emphasis, the unnecessary precision, the slight exaggeration that had to be defended later.

## 善數不用籌策

Good counting needs no tally sticks. 籌策 are the counting rods — the instrument of calculation.

The skill has become the thing itself. Which is not "he is so good he doesn't need tools," but: the count is held in the structure, not in the record.

## 善閉無關楗而不可開；善結無繩約而不可解

Good closing has no bolt and cannot be opened; good binding has no rope and cannot be untied.

This pair is the chapter's sharpest idea. A lock announces that there is something worth opening. A rope announces that there is a knot to work at.

What cannot be untied because there is no knot is not held by force; it is held by the arrangement. The thing is closed because it does not present itself as a door.

## 常善救人，故無棄人

> 是以聖人常善救人，故無棄人；常善救物，故無棄物.

The center of the chapter, and its weight is here rather than in the five skills.

無棄人 — no one is discarded. Not "everyone is treated kindly," but: there is no category of person that has been written off.

This is what the five skills are for. A person who leaves no tracks can approach without leaving a mark; a person who leaves no openings can speak without triggering defense; a person who binds without rope can hold a relation together without a contract.

A discarded person is usually one who was approached with tracks and openings — that is: with positions to defend.

## 襲明

> 是謂襲明.

襲 is to inherit, to receive a thing passed down — the same character used for inheriting a title. 明 is the clarity from chapter 16.

Not "enlightenment attained" but clarity received: the seeing that comes from the structure rather than from effort.

## 師與資

> 故善人者，不善人之師；不善人者，善人之資.

The good person is the teacher of the not-good; the not-good person is the resource of the good.

師 gives direction; 資 gives capital. The chapter is saying that the relation runs both ways, and that neither side is dispensable.

> 不貴其師，不愛其資，雖智大迷，是謂要妙.

Not valuing the teacher, not caring for the resource — clever as one may be, that is great confusion. This is called the essential subtlety.

要妙 — the essential subtlety. Not a mystical term: the hinge on which the whole chapter turns. The person who only takes from the "good" side and discards the other has cut off half of what is available.
